# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.

- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.

- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").

- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: Both groups hold answers that belong together (borrowing a pair to test first, and keeping up with many voices at once), the names are plain, and Diego's cost worry and Tomás's end-seat workaround fit neither group, so leaving them alone is right.
whys.g2: There is no junk or explicit answer on this line; Tomás's answer is off the question but sits on its own rather than in a group.

founder.order_why: Screen 14 (who else has to agree) belongs right after screen 10 (who decides and pays), but it sits after the cost and price screens, so the buyer question is split around them.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 10 and 14 both ask whether anyone besides the wearer decides on the purchase; screens 3 and 4 show the same kicker and question.
founder.missing: The price screen asks for one price, but AirCaps sells one-off glasses ($599) with an optional $20/month Pro plan, so I had to squash that into a yearly range. Nothing asks whether HSA/FSA money can pay for it, which is a real payer route for my buyers.

PRIMARY.order_why: The idea card and the order question are in the right places, but the price question sits under 'What you do today' and the count jumps from 2 of 5 to 4 of 5, so 3 of 5 seems to have gone missing.
PRIMARY.asked_twice: Screens 4 and 5 both ask what AirCaps is worth to me up front, the second just pushing for more.
PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked how I manage today: lipreading, asking people to repeat, a captioning app on my phone, an interpreter, or just nodding along. They also didn't ask where it goes wrong most, like noisy restaurants, family dinners, work meetings or the theatre, or whether I already wear glasses or hearing aids. And screen 3 asked about last month when I'd been told the study was about the last week.

screens.why1: Right after I said nobody else has to agree, it makes sense to show me back the people Keel will test before the stranger's question is built.
screens.why2: The intro repeats its own title ("The people involved. ... The people involved"), and the same wearer shown twice makes me stop and wonder whether Keel thinks the user and the buyer are two different people.
screens.why3: I know my buyers: the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult wears them and pays, often from their HSA/FSA, so this is squarely what I know.
screens.why4: "Has the problem" and "decides to buy" are two rows for the same person, so they overlap, and "Nobody else" carries no tag while the others do.
screens.why5: It still means what I typed: the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree; no role was added.
screens.why7: The belief (nobody else) matches my answer and no role was invented, but the card says the person with the problem and the decider share one row when they are the same person, and here they are split in two; "Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult" also runs past the 4-word cap.
screens.instead: One row to confirm: "Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult · has the problem and decides to buy" with "Nobody else · has to agree" above it, and the intro just "Keel used only the roles you named. Reword, remove or add; up to 4 words each."

screens.why1: Straight after I said nobody else has to agree, it makes sense to show me what Keel will test and let me confirm it or go back and name someone.
screens.why2: The belief is plain, but the bar's 'paid for something for this' is clumsy and the title runs two instructions together, so it takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know my wearers buy these themselves (HSA/FSA, the wearer pays), so confirming 'nobody else has to agree' comes straight from what I know.
screens.why4: A list holding only my own pick, Nobody else, with the way back to name a role, is exactly the choice I have here; nothing is missing or doubled.
screens.why5: It keeps what I picked: the wearer decides and nobody else has to agree, with no role I never named slipped in.
screens.why7: Per the card, a Nobody-else-only list is a statement to confirm; the belief says nobody else, the bar is 2 in 3 with only 'decided alone' counting for it, so it can hold or fail.
screens.instead: Keep it, but word the bar: Holds if at least 2 in 3 deaf or hard-of-hearing adults say they decided on their own the last time they paid for something like this.

screens.why1: After who decides and the price, asking what first step I'd want a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult to take before paying is the obvious next thing to pin down.
screens.why2: The question reads plainly, but the hint's examples ('pay for a pilot', 'let us run a trial') are B2B words that don't fit someone buying a pair of glasses, and 'where any money goes' needs a second read.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I'd ask a new wearer to do first: order the glasses on our 15-day risk-free returns.
screens.why4: The only chip is 'I'm not sure', which the card allows on the founder's side and which fits as a way to leave the dimension out.
screens.why5: My answer 'order the caption glasses with free returns' is kept whole, with the product and the free returns that define the step.
screens.why7: The box asks for one step in base form within 9 words, and my step names what it acts on and keeps 'free returns'; because it costs money, the hint correctly promises a smaller free step on the next screen, and 'I'm not sure' is allowed here.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take, and what would it cost them? (e.g. "order a pair with free returns" or "try a demo pair in a store")

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first step and its cost, Keel shows me how strangers will hear it before the belief is fixed, which is exactly where this check belongs.
screens.why2: The step itself reads plainly, but the smaller-step line is garbled as 'Yes, after A look at a working pair of caption glasses first', and the two word counters (7/9 and 9/9) make me read it twice to work out which is mine.
screens.why3: Whether a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult would order glasses on a returnable basis is exactly what I watch every day in our orders and returns.
screens.why4: The four answers are distinct and complete, but the soft yes 'Probably, after a look first' drops what they would look at, so a stranger hears 'a look' at nothing in particular.
screens.why5: My step 'order the caption glasses with free returns' is kept word for word in the step, the first yes and the belief, with no timing or number I did not write.
screens.why7: Measure, order, two-for-two balance and the absent escape all fit, and a money step rightly carries a free smaller step, but the soft yes is served as 'after a look first' rather than the card's 'Probably, after {smaller step} first', so one shape rule is bent.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order the caption glasses with free returns, or not? Yes, I'd order the caption glasses with free returns / Probably, after a look at a working pair first / Probably not / No

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step (order the caption glasses with free returns), asking whether to offer it to people who say yes at the end is the obvious next move before the study goes out.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with the hint showing the exact closing line and where I'll see the yeses is plain to me as a founder on first read.
screens.why3: Whether I want to collect emails from deaf and hard-of-hearing people willing to try the glasses is entirely my own call.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this decision, and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: The hint's line "Would you try this for real?" keeps the spirit of my step, but the screen doesn't show my step itself (order the caption glasses with free returns), so I can't confirm the pilot line respondents see carries it.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you order the caption glasses with free returns? Leave your email." -- Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who will put my questions to people belongs here, in the last step before the link goes out, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Two named interviewers with a five-second sample each, plus a credit cost and a text-message link, read plainly to a founder who has already paid for tools like this.
screens.why3: I can hear the two samples and pick, but for my people the voice matters least; whether the face is easy to lipread and the captions keep pace matters most, and the screen gives me nothing to judge that by.
screens.why4: Two voices are distinct, but for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents there is no choice that leads with text, such as a captions-first or silent interviewer, which is the one many of mine would want.
screens.why5: It keeps my actor's words, 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults', and leaks nothing of AirCaps to the respondent; the hint's 'voice' and my recorded 'face' differ only slightly.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Daphne ▶ / Saskia ▶ / Captions only, no voice (the question is written on screen and they type or tap). Hear each one and see how clear the face is for lipreading.

screens.why1: Once I've picked who asks, choosing how my wearers answer is the obvious next step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'asks aloud on video' and 'read and tap' are clear at a glance.
screens.why3: I know my people: many deaf and hard-of-hearing adults won't rely on spoken questions, so I can answer this from what I know of them.
screens.why4: Three distinct, complete choices; the AI option says every question is also written on screen, so it isn't closed to deaf respondents, and 'read and tap' is there for those who'd rather not use audio.
screens.why5: My pick, Read and tap, is kept as I made it and nothing of AirCaps leaks into the options.

screens.why1: Once I've picked how deaf and hard-of-hearing adults will answer, the next obvious thing is who gets the link, so this is the right last step before sending.
screens.why2: Each option says plainly what I'd do: send named links, use a Keel list, or post one link where people already gather, like an HLAA chapter group or a Deaf community forum.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I'd reach: the hard-of-hearing people I've met since the TranscribeGlass days, plus the community groups I could post in.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and cover the real ways I'd reach people (my own contacts, a sourced list, an open community post), and none is missing or overlapping.
screens.why5: Nothing here drifts from what I typed, and my pick of people I know by name is offered as written; nothing about the product or roles leaks.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right under the title with the deciding number beside it ('Existing sacrifice: 1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations'), and the 'worst of all its cards' rule explains why that card decides it.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows what is counted, over 7, and a 'bar 5 of 7', but I need a second look at 'Not reached ... nothing to ask', at 'per person a month' in the headline versus 'a month' on the card, and at the numbering that jumps from 4 to 6.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment are mine, but my cost estimate was $200 to $1,500 a year and here it is '12 conversations a month lost the thread of', and my $599 to $839 a year shows as $599 up front plus an optional $20, so I recognise them only as rewordings.
screens.why_b4: The status lines ('they value it below your price', 'smaller than you think') are generic, and nothing says what to do: rethink the $599 price, find who already spends, or test a cheaper entry point, even though 0 of 7 at $599 is the biggest news on the page.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible but is never called small, and 'Commitment: Holding up, 6 of 7 said yes' is shown without comment next to '0 of 7 at $599 or more', a soft overstatement of a free-returns yes that nobody would pay for at my price.
screens.instead: Not holding up on 7 people, a small sample: nobody valued AirCaps at $599 (0 of 7), and only 1 of 7 loses as much today as you estimated. The 6 of 7 who would order with free returns are not yet buyers at this price, so test a lower up-front price or find the people who already pay for captioning.

screens.why_b1: 'Not holding up' sits right beside '1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month · bar 5 of 7', so I know my belief failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: I can see seven cells, one for and six against, but the unit 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' is garbled share-frame wording, and a marker at 5 on a 0-to-15 axis reads like 5 conversations rather than 5 of 7 people, so I need a second look.
screens.why_b3: The card keeps my dimension and my 12 conversations, but it drops the 'per person' the stage page showed, and its 'lose ... conversations they lost the thread of' wording is clumsy, so I recognise it as mine reworded.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and points me to the Price card, but it never says what a lower cost means for AirCaps, such as leaning on the value of following the group rather than on a cost I assumed.
screens.why_b5: The count line says 'a lean, not a call', yet 'smaller than you think: they lose less today' states it flatly, and it rests on 'how many conversations fell through', which people may have read as cancelled plans rather than conversations whose thread they lost.
screens.instead: Not holding up, a lean from 7: 1 of 7 lost the thread of 12 or more conversations per person last month (most said 2 to 8), short of the 5 of 7 bar; your cost may be smaller than you thought, so see whether the Price card shows they'd pay anyway.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it, 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Both ladders show the count in each band, every cell marked for or against, my $599 and $20 marked as band low edges, and the strip putting all 7 against with the marker at 5, so I can read it at a glance.
screens.why_b3: 'Deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would think AirCaps worth $599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan' is my sticker price and my Pro plan, with the plan's 'optional' kept.
screens.why_b4: The So line says where they cluster ($250 to under $599, 6 of 7) and points to Insights, but it does not draw the concrete move the answers suggest: a lower entry price, or a loaner or demo pair before ordering, which three of them asked for.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is said, and nothing claims more than the data carries, though 'Fewer than 2 in 3' undersells a 0 of 7 and counting an optional plan as required could mislead on another result.
screens.instead: None of 7 would pay $599 up front, and 6 put it at $250 to under $599. On 7 people that is a lean, not a call: test an entry price under $599, or a loaner or demo pair before ordering, as three of them asked.

screens.why_b1: "Not reached" sits right beside "0 of 7 named your price or more · nothing to ask", so I know this card decides nothing and why: nobody got as far as my $599.
screens.why_b2: Three bars all at 0 are plain enough, but the strip shows 5 ghost cells while 7 people answered and no bar marker, so I need a second look to see that the 5 is the floor, not the people.
screens.why_b3: The card says "your belief", but I never checked this line: Keel derived it, rewrote my price as $599 up front then $20 a month, and turned my idea into "money they already spend on this", which I recognise but did not type.
screens.why_b4: "Ability to pay waits until at least 5 do" says what the card needs, not what I should do, which is to fix the price (all 7 sit below $599, six of them at $250 to under $599) before this question can be asked at all.
screens.why_b5: No claim beyond the data: n=7 is visible, everyone is listed as not asked with their band, and "Not reached" makes no call either way.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right on top with '6 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7' beside it, so I see the result and the number that decides it together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers with 6 for and 1 against, the count line says 7 answered and 7 counted, and the strip puts the marker at 5 of 7 (at least 2 in 3), so I get all three at a glance.
screens.why_b3: 'Buyer and payer' and 'the deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else must agree first' are what I picked when I chose Nobody else, and 'You said nobody else has to agree' restates it plainly.
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats the tally ('They decide alone... 1 of 7 needed someone's agreement'); it doesn't tell me that, with the wearer deciding alone, the blocker on this money stage is the price and the cost estimate, not who signs off.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and although the So line's 'They decide alone' reads a little flat, the hedge right above it keeps it honest.
screens.instead: Holding up, as a lean on 7: the wearer pays on their own, so selling direct to them is right; who decides isn't what's stopping the sale, the price is.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 said yes and bar 5 of 7, and with only 1 of 7 against, well under 1 in 3, the number plainly decides the verdict.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the seven answers across the four options, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against and my marker at 5, so what is counted, over how many and where the bar sits are all clear at first look.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and 'order the caption glasses with free returns' are the step I kept, and the belief line is mine word for word (the doubled 'Asked: Asked:' and the extra '— if it were offered today' are clutter, not a rewording).
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' reads like a pilot template; for a consumer order I don't know what I'm booking anyone into, and it says nothing about the price, which 0 of 7 would pay at $599 on the card I just read.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly says a small group gives a lean, not a call, but the So line then treats it as a call. A yes to an order with no price named and free returns can't carry 'book them in' against the Price card's 0 of 7.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 would order the caption glasses on free returns, but the question named no price and none of them valued it at $599, so a lean: send these six the order link at the real price and see who keeps the pair past the 15 days.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on Not holding up with 0 of 7 at $599 up front and 0 of 7 at $20 a month against a bar of 5 of 7, so the verdict and the number that decides it sit together.
screens.why_b3: Price and the belief line, $599 up front then an optional $20 a month plan, are exactly what I typed.
screens.why_b4: The group names hint at moves (let people try a pair, prove it keeps up with crosstalk), but the screen never says what the failed price means for the idea or what to change first.
screens.why_b5: The count line keeps n plain (7 against, 6 asked here, Amaka never saw it), each group shows its count of 2, and nothing is claimed beyond those six people.
screens.why_b6: I learn three things I did not type: people want to borrow a pair before buying even though I already offer 15-day free returns, the value hinges on catching many voices at once (audience questions, eleven people at a family lunch), and some live with a free workaround (the end seat, lipreading and laughing late), with most putting the monthly plan under $10.
screens.instead: Under the groups, say what it means: two want to try before buying, so put the 15-day free returns or a loaner up front; two would pay more if it handled many speakers, so prove that; and most value the plan under $10 a month, so test a lower plan price.

screens.why1: It's the first screen and it checks whether I'm someone who talks with hearing people regularly, which is the obvious thing to ask before anything else about those conversations.
screens.why2: 'Hearing people' is how I and everyone I know in the deaf and hard-of-hearing world say it, so I can answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know exactly how often I talk with hearing people at work, in shops and with family, so this is my own life.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and having no escape is right for a gate question like this.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's 'talk with hearing people every week' and shows me nothing of a product or the founder's own terms for me.
screens.why6: It is one short question I can take in at once, though the spoken form leaves off the 'Yes or no.' that a gate question should end on.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you talk face to face with hearing people? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, showing me the idea before asking about it makes sense; it isn't abrupt.
screens.why2: Captions, glasses, a lens and eye contact are all words I use about my own day; I got it on one read.
screens.why3: Losing the thread because I'm stuck between someone's mouth and a caption screen is exactly my life, so I can picture this.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown openly as an idea to imagine, says what it is and what they believe in plain words, and no product or role talk leaks past that.
screens.why6: Four short sentences with no slash, brackets or abbreviation say well; the repeated 'lightweight glasses' and 'people nearby' are a touch redundant but easy to hold.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that captions what people nearby say. While someone is talking, their words show as live captions inside the lens. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: After the screener about weekly talk with hearing people, asking how many conversations went wrong for me last month is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Fell through' sounds to me like a plan that got cancelled, not a conversation I couldn't follow or had to drop out of, so I'd have to read it twice to guess what they mean.
screens.why3: I know the conversations where I lost the thread or gave up and nodded along, but I don't keep a count, so I'd be guessing at a number for the month.
screens.why4: A number box labelled in conversations, plus None and I can't recall, covers every true answer without overlap.
screens.why5: 'Fell through' blurs whatever the founder meant (conversations I couldn't follow or join) into something vaguer, though nothing of the product leaks.
screens.why6: The question is short, but 'A number of conversations last month' is a fragment that sounds odd said aloud, and 'fell through' is no clearer heard than read.
screens.why7: It is a count in the founder's month, with the one escape and None as 0, but the verb is the 'fell through' the card says to avoid, so I can't be sure my number is the founder's measure.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations with hearing people did you stop being able to follow? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: After the idea card, asking what AirCaps would be worth makes sense, but it arrives right after a question about conversations falling through, under a 'What you do today' kicker, so it feels abrupt and mislabelled.
screens.why2: 'Up front' is plain to me, but the second step, 'And after that, what would it be worth to you a month?', never says what the monthly money pays for, so I'd have to stop and guess whether it's for the captions service or something else.
screens.why3: I buy my own hearing gear and pay for caption apps, so I know what I'd spend on glasses and a monthly service from my own wallet.
screens.why4: Both ladders are complete and don't overlap, each has 'I wouldn't pay for this', and 'I can't say' is the right single escape.
screens.why5: The odd $599 band edge, when every other edge is round, reads like a price tag someone already picked, and it hints at what the company plans to charge.
screens.why6: Each step reads four short options then 'Or say: I can't say', and the follow-up asks for only two bands, so I could hold it on one hearing.
screens.why7: This is a price-first-then-plan setup with two ladders of six; each has an edge exactly at the founder's low ($599, $20) with two bands below plus 'wouldn't pay' against and three bands for, all on one measure, and the escape is there.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? (Under $250 · $250 to under $599 · $599 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this), then: And for the captions service after that, what would it be worth to you a month? (same monthly bands)

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, asking what would push it higher is the natural next thing to ask me.
screens.why2: It reads my own answer back as I'd say it, about $250 to $600, and "what would make it worth more" is plain on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would make captioning glasses worth more to me, like working in a loud restaurant, keeping up when people talk over each other, or lasting a whole show, because I live those conversations every week.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was named on the idea card, so the name reaching me here is expected, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms shows through.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, and the dollar range says well aloud as two hundred fifty to six hundred dollars.

screens.why1: Right after I told them what AirCaps would be worth to me, asking who else had a say the last time I paid for something like it follows naturally.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself; 'something like this' makes me think of my hearing aids or my captioning app, which is close enough to answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know exactly who had a say when I bought my last hearing aids or caption phone, so this comes straight from my own life.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone to someone else deciding, and 'someone else had to agree' covers my insurer or my audiologist; 'I can't say' fits as the way out.
screens.why5: Nothing about the company's plans or its words for people reaches me, only AirCaps by the name I already saw on the idea card.
screens.why6: Heard once, it's one short question and four short answers I can hold, then the single way out.
screens.why7: With 'nobody else' tested, only 'I decided on my own' supports it and the other three refute it, in the card's order with its past-tense wording, and 'I can't say' is the one escape set apart.

screens.why1: After the price and who has to agree, asking whether I'd actually order the glasses is the obvious last question, even though the kicker still says 'What you do today' about something hypothetical.
screens.why2: 'Order the caption glasses with free returns' is how I'd say it myself, and I get it on one read.
screens.why3: I buy my own hearing gear and know how I'd go about ordering something like this, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: The four are distinct and complete, but 'after a look first' leaves me asking a look at what: a video, a demo, someone else's pair?
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's step whole, ordering with free returns, and 'caption glasses' is plain, not their jargon.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four options I can hold when I hear them once; only 'after a look first' sounds a little clipped aloud.
screens.why7: The first option is the founder's step whole and the soft yes is a real, smaller, free step, balanced two for and two against with no escape, but the smaller step 'a look' doesn't name what it acts on (the card's own good example says 'a look at how it works').
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order the caption glasses with free returns, or not? Yes, I'd order the caption glasses with free returns · Probably, after a look at how they work first · Probably not · No
